recipes.name: Chicken Paprikash
ingredients_raw: 1.5 pounds bone-in chicken pieces, with skin

steps.text: Make dumplings: Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil over high heat. Mix beaten eggs, 1/2 cup water, and salt together in a large bowl until well combined.
Gradually stir in flour to make a stiff batter.
Scoop up some batter with a spoon and use another spoon to scrape it into boiling water. Repeat until several dumplings are cooking together.
Cook until dumplings float to the top, about 10 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain in a colander or sieve. Rinse with warm water and drain again. Repeat to make remaining dumplings.
Make sauce: Melt butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add chicken and cook until lightly browned, 3 to 5 minutes per side.
Add onion and cook until translucent, 5 to 8 minutes.

Pour in water and season with paprika, black pepper, and salt. Continue to cook until chicken is no longer pink at the bone and the juices run clear, 10 to 15 more minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted near the bone should read at least 165 degrees F (74 degrees C). Remove chicken from the skillet and keep warm; leave liquid in the skillet.

Stir sour cream and flour together in a small bowl until well combined. Add to liquid in the skillet and slowly stir to combine. Bring to a boil, stirring constantly, and cook until thickened, 2 to 3 minutes.
Gently spoon dumplings into sauce and stir to coat. Cook until heated through, 2 to 3 minutes.
Spoon dumplings, sauce, and chicken onto serving plates.

raw_recipe.headline: Chicken Paprikash
raw_recipe.description: This chicken paprikash recipe with its colorful paprika-seasoned sour cream sauce is a variation of a classic chicken and dumpling casserole.

video.description: This Hungarian national dish will fill you up and keep you warm on a cold winter night. This variation of the famous paprika chicken gives you a taste of Hungarian orgin. Easy and delicious this is the perfect dish to go to for comfort food.

review.reviewBody: This was very good, I have made it twice.Both times I used bonless breast because thats what we always have on hand. the first time I used regular (spanish) Paprika, and it was pretty good. The second time i used Hungarian paprika, Oh my god what a difference. the second time i made it it was for 9 hungry firemen. They devoured it. I know alot of people say to make good paparikash you need to use bone in chicken, but i'm here to say that this was outstanding with bonless breast. I will be making this for years to come. Thanks for sharing

This is a great recipe - to add taste to the chicken, I salt the chicken and let it rest for at least an hour before cooking time. Chicken thighs are the best. Also, you can start with the onions, add a little water to them and no butter, cover the pot and cook them for 10-12 minutes. The onions will be translucent and you don't need the oil or butter. I also add a heaping Tablespoon of Penzy's Hungarian Sweet Paprika at this point. Then add the chicken. To give it a kick in flavor, I add a 14 oz can of diced tomatoes and green chilies and some cut up bell or other type of sweet pepper. This will add enough liquid that you won't need to add maybe 1/4 cup water. Once the cooking is done. Serve the Paprikas over the nokedli with a dallop of sour cream instead of putting it into the sauce. It tastes great even without the sour cream and the calories will be less. The nokedli can be made using a spetzel maker. My husband is Hungarian and these are the ways my family have made this dish our tradition.

I make this ALL the time. My father was Hungarian and gave us all the secrets. First, you have to dredge the chicken in flour with paprika, then put it in a hot skillet with butter to brown. I take out the chicken and put the pieces into the greased casserole dishes, THEN I put the onion into the pan with more butter and fry it until translucent. I add chicken broth and stir it around and pour it over the chicken in the casserole dishes. The most important thing IS, after cooking the chicken for about 45 minutes at 350, I take the chicken out of the casserole dishes and mix the sour cream into the broth and onion. I put the chicken back in and spoon some sauce over the chicken and cook for an additional 15-25 minutes. I make about 3 casserole dishes when I make it. By dredging the chicken in flour with paprika it helps to thicken the sauce.

This is really a good basic recipe. With my Matka and Babcia gone, I could not remember how to make it. I remember the flour dumplings(you can also use rye flour)..but cant remember the rest

Remember this is a stew, so it can be slkow cooked in a crock pot.

It's a great starter recipe.

Thoughts on how to make it better:
Dumplings: add 1 tsp garlic powder and 1 tsp onion powder to the recipe.

Sauce/liquid: 1/2 to 1 teaspoon HOT Hungarian Paprika and 1/2 teaspoon SMOKED paprika
1 teaspoon thyme
2 medium onions or 1 LARGE onion.

Sour Cream: mix the flour in very well and let stand in the sour cream for 5-10 minutes as it helps with the mix. You're actually making a thickened cream sauce.

**Note: for those folks who cannot have wheat or rye flour thickeners, you can use "Thicken Up" products and use the amount needed for pudding consistency.

To be fair, I haven't actually tried this recipe. That's because, it's the same recipe that my Hungarian Great Grandmother used to make for us and what I've cooked for the last 30 years. The only change I'd make is to use Hungarian Paprika. It will make a difference. Oh and I do cook my chicken longer in the broth so it's super tender. So delish!

This was delicious and I will definitely make it again! Love the flavor! The major things I changed was like the other reviewers, use chicken broth for everything instead of water and it's more flavorful like that. And I used skinless, boneless chicken breasts - saves some fat that way. I ended up cutting the dumplings to make them smaller after they were cooked as a personal preference. Be advised that the dumplings are time-consuming and you should do them in batches. Interesting thoughts from my husband and daughter - they thought the sauce tasted like a cheese sauce so I guess if you like cheese you'll probably like it. I just know that it was very tasty. My husband was watching me lick that sauce off the spoon when cleaning up! I'm sure it was delicious even without the changes. Thanks for sharing Erin!

This is a great recipe, but needed a couple tweaks. As some reviewers noted, I used chicken stock instead of water and added some half sharp hungarian paprika (Penzy's) along with the sweet. I did skip the dumplings and just served it over noodles. This is going into my recipe rotation. Reminded me of home.

Simple and delicious with chicken thighs. I used more paprika than called for and chicken broth instead of water. Also, I used spaetzel which made the process much easier than also making my own dumplings.

I'm a foodie, my husband is not. He had seconds, and then some, which is NOT TYPICAL at all! This dish is very good and reminds me of my beloved Aunt Jan's dish (she's passed on and I don't have her recipe). I don't understand some reviewer's comments on "bland". Perhaps they did not use butter and skin-on, bone-in chicken, and real sour cream. I used broth made from jarred chicken base so I reduced the salt (sea salt) to 1/4 t, used a cup or more of frozen chopped onion, freshly ground pepper, fresh Hungarian paprika, and added a little water from the wide egg noodles (I did not make the dumplings) to the sauce because my chicken wasn't done to at specified time so the liquid reduced further (which in turn, would have concentrated the flavors more). I had also stirred my flour into the onion mix to make a roux, then added the sour cream. It was an error on my part, but in retrospect, probably a good one because that would have pulled flour taste out (something I do when making any gravy).

I've been making this for years, since I ate it at a Hungarian restaurant in Toledo in the 70's. It's my husband's and both daughters' favorite, To save time,I usually serve it over tuxedo orzo. To save calories, I use about a TB of olive oil, then add the onions, add all the spices when they are softened, and then the chicken. I don't add water or flour anymore, though. I remove the chicken to a heated plate, then boil the liquid down to about 1/4 cup, turn off the heat and add light sour cream or plain yogurt (make sure it's not sweet) and blend it. Then add the chicken and turn to coat it. If you like it spicy, use smoked paprika. It's really good and authentic tasting.
Very good..skipped the dumplings and served over brown rice. Wanted it a bit spicier, so I added a teaspoon of garam masala!

Good flavor in sauce. Doesn't add seasoning to chicken at all! I used boneless, skinless breast instead of bone in because of preference. Added Tony's seasoning after played, AMAZING. Next time, I will double sauce recipe. Will definitely make again!

Didn’t follow it nearly to a T, but was a great general guide. Used boneless chicken breast, never combined the chicken AND dumplings until plating, and I believe the dumpling recipe is far off. Nowhere near wet enough to mix together. Believe some measurements were off. Great guide nonetheless
I will be making this again & again & again!! It's a TOTAL MOUTH PLEASER!!
I only have smoked paprika on hand and want to make this today... what are your thoughts on how that will affect the meal? Positive or negative?

Too much pepper, and sour cream. I would reduce the sour cream by about 1/4 cup per cup in the recipe. 3/4 cup sour cream and add 1/4 cup milk or cream. Up the flower just a bit. Do not add any pepper until the end, and then only to preference. Paprika varies, even though it's sweet, can still have some mild heat. You can add chicken broth (low salt) in place of the water. If you do don't add salt. I bought frozen Spatzles.
My husband loved it! Tweeked the "sauce" so he could have more of it. Honestly i think next time i make it i will use boneless skinless chicken thighs. It is just so much easier to eat.
